### Problem: Lucky Permutation {#sec-idx-p3-lucky}

::: {.p-statement}
You are given a permutation $p$ of $1..n$. In one operation you may swap any two elements. Find the minimum number of operations after which $p$ has **exactly one inversion** (exactly one pair $i < j$ with $p_i > p_j$). Constraints: $t \le 10^4$, $2 \le n \le 2 \cdot 10^5$, sum of $n$ at most $2 \cdot 10^5$. Samples: $[2, 1] \to 0$; $[1, 2] \to 1$; $[3, 4, 1, 2] \to 3$; $[2, 4, 3, 1] \to 1$.

Source: [CF 1768D · Lucky Permutation](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/1768/D){.solved rating="1800"}
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
A permutation with exactly one inversion is the identity with one adjacent pair $(k, k+1)$ swapped. Sorting costs $n - c$ swaps ($c$ = number of cycles). If some $k$ and $k + 1$ lie on the same cycle, stop one swap early and leave them as a 2-cycle: $n - c - 1$. Otherwise one extra swap is unavoidable: $n - c + 1$.
:::

::: {.p-approach}
1. **Breadth-first search over permutations.** For tiny $n$, search from $p$ with one edge per swap until a permutation with one inversion appears. $O(n! \cdot n^2)$: the oracle.
2. **Cycles plus one adjacent test.** Label every index with its cycle (one walk per cycle, as in @sec-idx-p3-books) and count the cycles $c$. If some $k$ has `comp[k] == comp[k+1]`, answer $n - c - 1$; else $n - c + 1$.

**Why this is optimal.** A permutation with one inversion has a single non-trivial cycle, the transposition $(k\ k{+}1)$, so it has $n - 1$ cycles. A swap changes the cycle count by exactly $\pm 1$ (@sec-idx-a4). From $c$ cycles, reaching $n - 1$ cycles needs at least $n - 1 - c$ swaps, with equality only if *every* swap splits a cycle. Splitting only refines the partition of indices into cycles: two indices that start on different cycles can never end on the same one. So if $k$ and $k + 1$ share a cycle, split everything else off and keep them together, $n - 1 - c$ swaps. If no adjacent pair shares a cycle, at least one swap must merge, and that merge must be paid back by an extra split, so at least $n - 1 - c + 2 = n - c + 1$ swaps are needed; sorting fully ($n - c$ swaps) and then swapping one adjacent pair achieves it.

**Worked trace.** $[2, 4, 3, 1]$: cycles $1 \to 2 \to 4 \to 1$ and the fixed point $3$, so $c = 2$. Indices $1$ and $2$ share a cycle, so the answer is $4 - 2 - 1 = 1$ (swap the values $4$ and $1$: $[2, 1, 3, 4]$). For $[3, 4, 1, 2]$ the cycles are $\{1, 3\}$ and $\{2, 4\}$: no adjacent pair shares one, so $4 - 2 + 1 = 3$.
:::

::: {#fig-idx-p3-lucky}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    rows = []
    for perm in ([2, 4, 3, 1], [3, 4, 1, 2]):
        comp, k = [None] * 4, 0
        for s in range(4):
            if comp[s] is None:
                j = s
                while comp[j] is None:
                    comp[j] = k
                    j = perm[j] - 1
                k += 1
        share = [i for i in range(3) if comp[i] == comp[i + 1]]
        rows.append((perm, comp, k, share))
    assert rows[0][3] == [0] and rows[1][3] == []
    palette = ["indigo", "green", "amber", "cyan"]
    for r, (perm, comp, c, share) in enumerate(rows):
        ans = 4 - c - 1 if share else 4 - c + 1
        V.array(ax, p, perm, y=-3.2 * r, label=f"p = {perm}",
                colors={i: palette[comp[i]] for i in range(4)},
                note=(f"c = {c}; indices {share[0] + 1},{share[0] + 2} share a cycle -> {ans}" if share
                      else f"c = {c}; no adjacent pair shares a cycle -> {ans}"))
V.show(draw)
```

Colours are cycles. In $[2, 4, 3, 1]$ the first two positions share the indigo cycle, so sorting can stop one swap early with them still swapped: answer $1$. In $[3, 4, 1, 2]$ neighbours always differ in colour, so a merge is forced: answer $3$.

:::

The buttons are in order. Each one keeps the previous solution and changes only what that form changes.

::: {.panel-tabset .solution-forms}

#### Breadth-first search over permutations

::: {.form-next}
Treat permutations as nodes and swaps as edges; the answer is the distance from $p$ to the nearest permutation with one inversion. Exponential, for $n \le 6$ only: the oracle.
:::

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}

##### Python

```{python}
def inversions(p):
    return sum(1 for i in range(len(p)) for j in range(i + 1, len(p)) if p[i] > p[j])


def lucky_brute(p):
    start = tuple(p)
    dist = {start: 0}
    queue = [start]
    for u in queue:                      # the list grows while we scan it: a FIFO queue
        if inversions(u) == 1:
            return dist[u]
        for i in range(len(u)):
            for j in range(i + 1, len(u)):
                v = list(u)
                v[i], v[j] = v[j], v[i]
                v = tuple(v)
                if v not in dist:
                    dist[v] = dist[u] + 1
                    queue.append(v)


assert [lucky_brute(p) for p in ([2, 1], [1, 2], [3, 4, 1, 2], [2, 4, 3, 1])] == [0, 1, 3, 1]
```

##### C++

```cpp
int luckyBrute(vector<int> p) {                     // n <= 6
    auto inv = [](const vector<int>& v) {
        int c = 0;
        for (size_t i = 0; i < v.size(); i++)
            for (size_t j = i + 1; j < v.size(); j++) c += v[i] > v[j];
        return c;
    };
    map<vector<int>, int> dist;
    queue<vector<int>> q;
    dist[p] = 0;
    q.push(p);
    while (!q.empty()) {
        vector<int> u = q.front(); q.pop();
        if (inv(u) == 1) return dist[u];
        for (size_t i = 0; i < u.size(); i++)
            for (size_t j = i + 1; j < u.size(); j++) {
                vector<int> v = u;
                swap(v[i], v[j]);
                if (!dist.count(v)) { dist[v] = dist[u] + 1; q.push(v); }
            }
    }
    return -1;
}
```

:::

#### Cycles plus one adjacent test

::: {.form-next}
Label each index with its cycle in one $O(n)$ pass and count the cycles. One more pass over adjacent pairs decides between $n - c - 1$ and $n - c + 1$.
:::

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}

##### Python

```{python}
def lucky(p):
    n = len(p)
    comp = [-1] * n
    c = 0
    for s in range(n):
        if comp[s] < 0:
            j = s
            while comp[j] < 0:
                comp[j] = c
                j = p[j] - 1
            c += 1
    if any(comp[k] == comp[k + 1] for k in range(n - 1)):
        return n - c - 1
    return n - c + 1


assert [lucky(p) for p in ([2, 1], [1, 2], [3, 4, 1, 2], [2, 4, 3, 1])] == [0, 1, 3, 1]
for n in range(2, 6):                    # every permutation up to n = 5 ...
    for perm in itertools.permutations(range(1, n + 1)):
        assert lucky(list(perm)) == lucky_brute(list(perm)), perm
for _ in range(15):                      # ... and random ones of length 6
    perm = random.sample(range(1, 7), 6)
    assert lucky(perm) == lucky_brute(perm), perm
```

##### C++

```cpp
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;

int main() {
    int t;
    scanf("%d", &t);
    while (t--) {
        int n;
        scanf("%d", &n);
        vector<int> p(n), comp(n, -1);
        for (int& x : p) { scanf("%d", &x); x--; }
        int c = 0;
        for (int s = 0; s < n; s++)
            if (comp[s] < 0) {
                for (int j = s; comp[j] < 0; j = p[j]) comp[j] = c;
                c++;
            }
        bool share = false;
        for (int k = 0; k + 1 < n; k++) share |= comp[k] == comp[k + 1];
        printf("%d\n", share ? n - c - 1 : n - c + 1);
    }
    return 0;
}
```

:::

:::

::: {.p-complexity}
**Breadth-first search over permutations:** $O(n! \cdot n^2)$ time and $O(n! \cdot n)$ memory. **Cycles plus one adjacent test:** $O(n)$ time, $O(n)$ space for the cycle labels.
:::

::: {.p-edge}
- Already one inversion ($[2, 1]$, or the identity with one adjacent swap): $c = n - 1$ and the swapped pair shares its cycle, so $n - c - 1 = 0$.
- The identity: $c = n$, no pair shares a cycle, so $n - c + 1 = 1$. Sorted is *not* the target; one adjacent swap is needed.
- The cycles are taken over *positions* ($i \to p_i$). Positions $k$ and $k + 1$ on one cycle is the test, because the target keeps value $k$ at position $k$ except for the swapped pair.
- There are $n - 1$ possible targets, one per adjacent pair; the test above takes the best of them at once, so no target has to be tried separately.
- Use the swap-changes-cycles-by-one fact, not "count misplaced elements": $[3, 4, 1, 2]$ has four misplaced elements but needs only three swaps.
:::
